title: Ezekiel
subtitle: the glory that left, and the glory that came back
lead: Ezekiel was a priest from Jerusalem who was carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin and thousands of other Judeans. Five years later, by a canal in Babylonia, he saw the heavens open: a storm cloud, four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with a figure like a human being on it. This was the glory of the LORD, and it had come to the exiles, outside the land and outside the Temple. The book that follows is the strangest and most carefully dated of the prophets. Its visions and sign acts are told in the first person, and God calls the prophet "son of man" about ninety times.

The book has three parts. Chapters 1 to 24 are judgment on Jerusalem, which the exiles believed could not fall. Chapters 25 to 32 are oracles against the nations around Judah: Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and Sidon, and then seven oracles against Egypt. Chapters 33 to 48 begin on the night a survivor reaches Babylon with the news that the city has fallen, and turn to hope: shepherds and sheep, a new heart, dry bones that live, the defeat of Gog, and a new Temple to which the glory returns. One refrain runs through all of it, in more than sixty verses, in slightly different dress each time: "Then they will know that I am the LORD."
facts: The book names Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest (1:3), and is written mostly in his voice ("I"). The Talmud says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote it down (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a). Modern scholars divide between those who think the book is mostly the prophet's own work and those who see later hands (see "How the book was made").

The first vision is dated to the fifth year of the exile of Jehoiachin, 593 BC (1:1-2). The latest dated oracle is in the twenty-seventh year, 571 BC (29:17), and the Temple vision of chapters 40-48 is dated to 573 (40:1). The book never says what became of Ezekiel.

Tel-abib, a village of Judean exiles by the Kebar canal in Babylonia (3:15), probably near Nippur in what is now southern Iraq. The exiles had come in 597 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle dates the capture of Jerusalem to the second of Adar (about 16 March 597). Ezekiel speaks to them in their houses and acts out messages for them, but his oracles are often about the people still in Jerusalem.

Prophecy in many shapes: visions (1-3; 8-11; 37; 40-48), sign acts the prophet performed (4-5; 12; 24; 37:15-28), long allegories (15; 16; 17; 23), laments (19; 26-28; 32), debate speeches (18; 33:10-20) and oracles against the nations (25-32). Most of it is prose, with real poetry in the laments and in the sword songs of 7 and 21.
Hebrew, with a number of rare words and some borrowed from Akkadian, the language of Babylon. It is among the hardest Hebrew in the Bible. The Greek translation is a literal one.

48 chapters, 1,273 verses. English and Hebrew verse numbers differ only in one place, English 20:45-49, which is Hebrew 21:1-5, and English 21:1-32, which is Hebrew 21:6-37. This site uses English numbers throughout.

No prophet is dated as carefully. The book gives thirteen date formulas (1:1-2; 8:1; 20:1; 24:1; 26:1; 29:1; 29:17; 30:20; 31:1; 32:1; 32:17; 33:21; 40:1). They are counted in years from Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC, so the fifth year (1:2) is 593 BC, the sixth (8:1) is 592, the ninth (24:1) is 588 and the twelfth (33:21) is 586/585. The book is not in date order: 29:17 (571) comes before 30:20 (587).

Six copies of Ezekiel were found at Qumran and one at Masada: 1QEzek (1Q9), 3QEzek (3Q1), 4QEzek-a (4Q73), 4QEzek-b (4Q74), 4QEzek-c (4Q75), 11QEzek (11Q4) and Masada Ezekiel (Mas 1d), which has 35:11-38:14. They agree closely with the Masoretic Text. The oldest Greek copy is Papyrus 967, from about the early AD 200s, and its text differs from the Hebrew in order and length in places. The Leningrad Codex (AD 1008) is the base of this translation.

In Jewish Bibles it is the third of the Latter Prophets, after Isaiah and Jeremiah, though one Talmud passage lists Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b). Protestant Bibles put it after Lamentations and before Daniel. Catholic Bibles put Baruch between Lamentations and Ezekiel; Orthodox Bibles, which keep the Greek order, have Jeremiah, Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter of Jeremiah before it.

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads each oracle against the dates the book gives and the events it names: the deportation of 597, the siege that began in 588, the fall of Jerusalem in 586, Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Tyre and his later campaign in Egypt. It asks what happened to what Ezekiel announced, including the oracle of 29:17-20, which admits that one prediction did not come out as planned.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made and where it was written: the old debate over one author or many, the layers that scholars such as Zimmerli find, the Babylonian setting against the Palestinian one, the Greek text that is shorter than the Hebrew, the parallels with the Holiness Code in Leviticus, and the images that Babylonian art and religion supply for the visions.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: How the Targum, the rabbis and the medieval commentators (Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra) read Ezekiel: the haftarah for Shavuot, the Account of the Chariot that the sages limited to a few students, the problem of a Temple in chapters 40-48 whose laws differ from the Torah, and the long Jewish hope of a rebuilt Temple. The Jewish mystics of the Hekhalot and Merkavah writings begin from chapter 1.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: How the church fathers, the Reformers and later Christians read Ezekiel: the four faces and the four Gospels, the shepherd of chapter 34 fulfilled in Jesus, the new heart and spirit of chapter 36 and the new birth, the dry bones and the resurrection, and the Temple of chapters 40-48 as the church, as Christ, or as a future building.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads the later chapters as unfinished: Gog of Magog (38-39) as a battle still ahead, the dry bones and the two sticks (37) as Israel's return in the last days, and the Temple and land of chapters 40-48 as a plan for a future kingdom. Christians and Jews both hold forms of this view, and they disagree widely with one another and with the other lenses.

audience.to: Ezekiel's first hearers were the Judeans deported to Babylonia in 597 BC, and above all the elders who came to sit in his house at Tel-abib (8:1; 14:1; 20:1). They were priests, officials, soldiers and craftsmen, taken with King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:14-16). Many of his oracles are about the people left in Jerusalem and Judah, who are spoken of but not spoken to. After the city fell in 586 BC (33:21), Ezekiel spoke to a broken community that now had to decide what its God was doing. The book as we have it was then read by exiles and by their children, and in time by Jews in the land under Persian rule, who read the Temple chapters in a world without a Temple.
audience.why: Before 586 the exiles believed the exile was short. Prophets in Babylon said so (Jeremiah 29:8-9), and Jerusalem and its Temple seemed safe because the LORD lived there. Ezekiel's message was the opposite: the city would fall, the Temple would be defiled and abandoned, and the exile was the people's own doing. After 586 the same book turns to hope: the LORD will gather his scattered flock, give his people a new heart and put his Spirit in them, and the glory that left the Temple will return. The recurring line, "Then they will know that I am the LORD," tells both audiences that what happens is the LORD's doing, whether it is judgment or restoration. Knowing who was listening explains why a priest acted out sieges and famine in front of men who did not want to hear it, and why, from the day he was struck mute (3:26) until the news of the fall reached him (33:22), about seven and a half years, he spoke only when the LORD gave him words.
views: Ezekiel in Babylon, for the exiles (the traditional and the common modern view)

Nearly all readers from the ancient world to the present take the book at its word: Ezekiel lived among the exiles in Babylonia, and he spoke to them. This view explains why he is told to act his messages out and why the elders sit before him. It is held by Jewish and Christian tradition and by Zimmerli, Greenberg, Block and Joyce, who differ on how much of the book is his own words.
Ezekiel in Jerusalem, or in both places

Some scholars, such as Alfred Bertholet (1936) and Volkmar Herntrich (1932), argued that the book shows a prophet at work in Jerusalem and that the Babylonian setting was added later. They pointed to oracles that seem to speak to a crowd that can hear him, such as the oracles about the Temple's sins in chapter 8. Few scholars hold this now, but some accept that Ezekiel may have visited, or been closely informed about, events in Judah.
A book written later and set in the exile

C. C. Torrey (1930) argued that the book was written around 230 BC and given a fictional setting in Babylon. Almost no one follows him today. Ben Sira, writing about 180 BC, already counts Ezekiel among the great prophets (Sirach 49:8-9), which leaves little time for a book written about 230 BC to have become famous, and Avi Hurvitz's linguistic work places the book's Hebrew in the sixth century rather than the third.

authorship: The prophet himself, in one scheme

The book presents itself as Ezekiel's own report: "I" speaks in nearly every chapter, and the dates run from his own call. Moshe Greenberg (Anchor Bible, 1983 and 1997) read the book as a whole, with a unified design from beginning to end, and called this a holistic reading. Daniel Block (NICOT, 1997 and 1998) holds that the book is mostly the prophet's own work, shaped by him and a few helpers in the exile. Paul Joyce (2007) also reads it as largely his own, while allowing for some later additions. The Talmud has a different but compatible idea: the Men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel down (Bava Batra 15a). Josephus says Ezekiel left behind two books about the captivity (Antiquities 10.5.1).

Walther Zimmerli (Hermeneia, 1979 and 1983) held that the core of each section goes back to Ezekiel, and that his disciples then expanded, applied and updated the sayings over decades, so that the book grew by layers. This is now the most widely used critical model. Zimmerli found the clearest later growth in the Temple chapters, but he still treated even those as developing the prophet's own vision.

Gustav Hölscher (1924) argued that only a small part of the book, mostly the poems, was the prophet's and that a later editor wrote most of the prose. Torrey (1930) said the whole book was a pseudepigraph from about 230 BC. Herntrich and Bertholet moved the setting to Jerusalem. These views shaped the field's early twentieth-century debates, and each made scholars notice a real feature of the book: the sudden changes of voice, the repeated sections, and the way some oracles seem to know the city's streets.
What the debate is not about

Everyone in this debate treats Ezekiel as a prophetic book. No one in it argues that Ezekiel was a fiction or a fraud, and the debate over layers does not change the book's date range or its claims to speak for the LORD. The question is how and when the words reached their present shape.
outline: The call: the storm, the four living creatures, the wheels and the throne; the scroll; sent to a rebellious house
The watchman; shut in the house and made mute
Sign acts of the siege: the brick, the iron plate, the days on his side, the bread, the shaved hair; Jerusalem in the middle of the nations
Oracles to the mountains of Israel; "an end, the end has come"
The Temple vision: four abominations, the slaughter, the glory leaves, the new heart
Exile sign acts; false prophets; elders with idols in their hearts; Noah, Daniel and Job
The useless vine; the foundling bride; the two eagles; individual responsibility; laments for the princes
The history of rebellion; the sword; the bloody city; Oholah and Oholibah; the pot; the death of the prophet's wife and the siege begins
Oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and Sidon; the king of Tyre and Eden
Seven oracles against Egypt; the great crocodile; the descent to Sheol
The watchman again; news of the fall; the people who hear and do not do
The shepherds of Israel and the LORD the shepherd
Mount Seir; the mountains of Israel renewed; the holy name; the new heart and spirit
The valley of dry bones; the two sticks
Gog of Magog and the return of Israel
The visionary tour of the new Temple; the return of the glory
The closed east gate; priests and Levites; the leader; festivals and offerings
The river from the Temple; the borders and tribal portions; "The LORD Is There"

sections.b:
The Plain English is made from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (the Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), one verse at a time, starting from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew. Verse numbers are the English ones. Where the Hebrew is very hard, the Plain gives the likeliest sense and a note says what the other possibilities are. Ezekiel repeats himself on purpose, so the Plain keeps the repetition: the same words open an oracle, and the same sentence ends it.

A few words are fixed across the whole book. God is the "Lord GOD" in 217 places where the Hebrew has Adonai YHWH, and God's address to the prophet is always "son of man". The Hebrew gillulim is "filthy idols", shiqqutsim is "detestable things" and to'evot is "abhorrent things", so that three Hebrew words stay three. The chief refrain is always "Then they will know that I am the LORD" ("you will know" when God speaks to the people), and a variant, "that I, the LORD, have spoken," shows where the Hebrew changes it.

Each chapter page says which witnesses the writer read directly: the Hebrew text and its marginal readings on this site, the Dead Sea Scrolls through the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions, and the Greek in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus. Later translations and the Greek critical editions of Rahlfs and Ziegler are cited only as reported by commentaries.

Ezekiel was a priest, and the book gives his father's name, Buzi, but no more of his family. The Hebrew name Yechezqel means "God strengthens" or "may God strengthen." In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, put Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah on the throne and deported the king, the royal household, the army officers and the skilled workers (2 Kings 24:10-17). Ezekiel went with them. The "thirtieth year" of 1:1 may be his age, which is the oldest view (Origen and Jerome held it), so that he was thirty, the age at which Levites began their service (Numbers 4:3), when the heavens opened. Others count the thirty years from another event, and none of the proposals is certain. The exiles were settled in villages by the canals of southern Babylonia, and later Babylonian records from Nippur mention a canal called the Kebar. They kept their families, ran their own affairs under their elders, and could receive letters from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 29:1-3).

The book ties Ezekiel's life to the signs he performs. He lies on his side for months (4:4-8), shaves his head (5:1-4), digs through a wall at night with his luggage (12:1-16) and does not mourn when his wife dies (24:15-27). He is made unable to speak, except when the LORD gives him a message (3:26-27; 24:27; 33:22). Some modern writers explained these acts as signs of mental illness, and the diagnoses (catalepsy, paranoia, others) belong to a modern tradition of interpretation with its own critics, who point out that prophets in Israel and elsewhere did unusual things on purpose (see 4:1-5:4). The book does not tell us how he died.

Ezekiel is one of the most orderly of the prophetic books. Its dated visions run mostly in order, its language repeats from chapter to chapter, and its first-person voice is steady. That led many scholars to say the book comes from one hand, and others to say the opposite: that such a book must have been made by a careful later editor who imitated the prophet. Both views are old. The Talmud's report that Hananiah son of Hezekiah needed three hundred jars of lamp oil to reconcile the book with the Torah (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 13b) shows that the book was already a puzzle in Jewish tradition.

The modern debate has these main positions. Hölscher (1924) said little of the prose was Ezekiel's. Torrey (1930) said the whole was written about 230 BC. Herntrich (1932) and Bertholet (1936) argued for a Palestinian setting. Zimmerli's two-volume commentary (1979, 1983) became the model for a prophet whose words were expanded by a school. Greenberg (1983, 1997) answered with a reading that finds a single design in the whole. Block (1997, 1998) and Joyce (2007) hold that the book is mainly the prophet's own work, and Joyce and others allow later notes and additions. Behind these views sits the question of how Ezekiel's priestly language relates to the Torah's Holiness Code (Leviticus 17-26): whether Ezekiel draws on it, or it on him, or both on a common stream. Scholars such as Avi Hurvitz (1982) argue from the form of the Hebrew that the priestly writings are earlier than Ezekiel, and others disagree. The question is open.

What the debate is not about is whether the book is prophetic. It is, in every reading, a collection of oracles and visions that claim to come from the LORD, set in the exile and ordered by dates.

sections.h: The Hebrew, Qumran and the Greek
sections.b:
The Qumran copies of Ezekiel agree closely with the Masoretic Text. In chapters 1 to 7 the scrolls that survive are 11QEzek (1:8-10; 4:3-6, 9-10; 5:11-17; 7:9-12), 4QEzek-b (1:10-13, 16-24) and 1QEzek (4:16-5:1). They show spelling differences and a few small ones in wording, and none that changes the meaning. A Masada scroll of Ezekiel preserves 35:11-38:14, and its text matches the Masoretic Text almost exactly.

The Greek is the main outside witness. Ezekiel's Greek is a literal translation, and scholars since H. St. J. Thackeray (1903) have argued that more than one translator worked on it. It is shorter than the Hebrew in places, mostly by single words and phrases. The oldest Greek manuscript, Papyrus 967 (from about the early AD 200s), is also the most debated. It is reported to leave out 12:26-28, to put chapter 37 after chapters 38-39 and to lack 36:23c-38, and these differences are discussed by Johan Lust (1981) and Emanuel Tov (1986), whom later writers in this book cite. Whether the Hebrew arrangement or the one in 967 is earlier is disputed.

Ezekiel is built around the glory of the LORD (kavod YHWH). The glory appears to him in Babylon in chapter 1, leaves the Temple step by step in chapters 8-11 and returns to the new Temple in chapter 43. Other threads run beside it. The LORD acts "for the sake of my name," which the people have profaned (20:9, 14, 22; 36:20-23). The recognition formula "Then they will know that I am the LORD" ends oracles of judgment and of rescue alike. Each person answers for their own life (18; 3:16-21; 33), the watchman must warn (3:16-21; 33:1-9), and the LORD will give a new heart and put his Spirit in his people (11:19-20; 36:26-27). The last chapters give a Temple, a city and a land with fixed borders, and the name of the city is "The LORD Is There" (48:35).

Ezekiel is read in the synagogue on Shavuot, the feast of weeks: the first day's haftarah (the prophet's reading after the Torah) is Ezekiel 1:1-28 with 3:12. The Mishnah restricts the teaching of the "Account of the Chariot" (Ezekiel 1) to one student at a time, and only if he is wise and understands on his own (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1). The Talmud tells of a boy who understood the word chashmal and was consumed by fire, so that the sages wanted to hide the book (Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 13a). The Mishnah also records a dispute over whether the chariot chapter may be read as a haftarah (Mishnah Megillah 4:10). Later Jewish mystics, in the Hekhalot ("Palaces") and Merkavah writings, sought to ascend to the throne of chapter 1. Maimonides in the Guide of the Perplexed (3.1-7) read the chariot as a picture of the order of the universe and the knowledge of God.

The Temple chapters were the hardest part. Their laws on sacrifice and the priesthood differ from the Torah's, and the sages could not reconcile them in every case. The Talmud tells that Hananiah son of Hezekiah did so for the book at the cost of three hundred jars of oil (Shabbat 13b), and it leaves other differences for "Elijah" to settle when he returns (for example Menachot 45a). Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra each read the book their own way, and the Targum of Ezekiel renders it with much expansion, especially in chapter 1. Ezekiel's vision of dry bones and of the Temple stays alive in Jewish hope of the resurrection and of a rebuilt Temple, with the readings and their disagreements described at those chapters.

sections.h: Ezekiel in the New Testament and the church
sections.b: Revelation draws heavily on Ezekiel: the throne and the four living creatures (Revelation 4:6-8, with Isaiah 6), the scroll that tastes sweet (Revelation 10:8-11, compare Ezekiel 2:8-3:3), the mark on the forehead (Revelation 7:3, compare Ezekiel 9:4), Gog and Magog (Revelation 20:8), the measured city with its twelve gates (Revelation 21:12-13, compare Ezekiel 48:30-35) and the river from the throne (Revelation 22:1-2, compare Ezekiel 47:1-12). Jesus' words about the good shepherd (John 10) answer Ezekiel 34. The church fathers read the four faces as the four Gospels: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8) matched them one way and Jerome (Preface to Matthew) another, and Jerome's matching of man, lion, ox and eagle with Matthew, Mark, Luke and John is the one later art follows. Origen preached on Ezekiel, and Jerome wrote a commentary on it (about AD 410 to 414). Gregory the Great preached twenty-two homilies on Ezekiel about AD 593, twelve of them on the opening chapters and ten on chapter 40. For the later chapters see the Christian readings under "Where Christians differ."

Three writings outside the Bible carry Ezekiel's name. Ezekiel the Tragedian wrote a Greek play on the Exodus, the Exagoge, probably in Alexandria in the second century BC; he is not the prophet. The Apocryphon of Ezekiel is a lost work that early Christian writers quote. Pseudo-Ezekiel is a set of fragments from Qumran that retell Ezekiel's visions, including the dry bones, in his voice. None of these is in any Bible. Another book often linked to Ezekiel's themes is the Qumran New Jerusalem text, which measures a future city much as Ezekiel 40-48 does.

The first seven chapters give the prophet's call and the first sign acts of judgment. Chapter 1 is a vision. Chapters 2 and 3 are the commission, with the eaten scroll and the watchman. Chapters 4 and 5 are acted messages: the prophet lies on his side, eats a rationed diet, cuts his hair and burns, strikes and scatters it. The listeners are the exiles, but the message is about Jerusalem. Chapter 6 speaks to the mountains of the land, and chapter 7 is a poem of the end. The first words of each oracle, "The word of the LORD came to me," appear again and again. Read the chapters aloud if you can: the sounds and the repetition are part of how they work.

reading: Moshe Greenberg, Ezekiel 1-20 and Ezekiel 21-37, Anchor Bible 22 and 22A (1983, 1997)
A careful close reading by a Jewish scholar who argues that the book has a single design.
The great critical commentary, with a full study of the text and of the layers Zimmerli finds in it.
Daniel I. Block, The Book of Ezekiel, 2 vols., New International Commentary on the Old Testament (1997, 1998)
A thorough evangelical commentary that treats the book as largely the prophet's own, with long essays on the visions.
A shorter commentary that asks what the book meant to people living through the exile.
Jon D. Levenson, Theology of the Program of Restoration of Ezekiel 40-48 (1976)
The standard study of the last nine chapters and their place in Jewish thought.
prompts: The vision by the Kebar canal (1:4-28)

A man in a plain wool robe stands by a wide canal in a flat, dry landscape of mud-brick huts and date palms. A huge storm cloud rolls in from the north, lit from inside by flashing fire. Out of it come four winged living creatures, each with four faces in the same drawn outline: a human, a lion, an ox and an eagle. Beside each creature is a wheel within a wheel, the rims covered with eyes. Above them hangs a pale dome like ice, and above that a blue throne with a glowing figure and a rainbow around it. Draw it in thick ink strokes like a cave painting, in warm ochre and deep blue, fading into the cracked texture of an old scroll with no hard edges.
The scroll that tasted like honey (2:8-3:3)

A young priest kneels in a dusty yard with his mouth open. An enormous hand reaches down from the top of the picture and holds out a long unrolled scroll, written on both sides with tiny lines of script that spill off the edges. Honey colors run through the page. The sky is flat and pale. Draw it as a sketch on aged parchment with soft, torn edges.

A man lies on his left side on bare ground before a clay brick with a small walled city scratched into it. Around the brick are tiny mounds, a ramp, tents and battering rams drawn like toys. A flat iron plate stands upright between him and the brick like a wall, and ropes lie across his shoulders. Neighbors watch from the doorways of nearby houses. Use thin brown ink lines, a faded wash of red and gray, and edges that dissolve into the grain of a scroll.

traditions.q: What is the Temple of Ezekiel 40-48?
views: A real temple will be built in a future kingdom of Christ on earth, and Ezekiel's plan describes it. The sacrifices in it are taken as memorials that look back to the cross, as the Lord's Supper does. This is the reading in the Scofield Reference Bible's notes on these chapters and in John Walvoord's The Millennial Kingdom. Not every dispensationalist takes the sacrifices the same way.

The vision is a picture, in the Old Testament's own images, of God dwelling with his people, and it is fulfilled in Christ and the church rather than in a building. Hebrews 8 to 10 says the old sacrifices are finished, and Revelation 21:22 sees no temple in the new Jerusalem. G. K. Beale (The Temple and the Church's Mission) reads Ezekiel's temple as a pointer to the temple that grows to fill the world, and Anthony Hoekema (The Bible and the Future) takes the amillennial view of such visions as pictures of the new creation.

The church fathers read the measured temple as the church and as the soul: Jerome in his Commentary on Ezekiel, and Gregory the Great in his homilies on chapter 40, which lead the reader through the building as a way of climbing in the spiritual life. The Catechism uses the temple image for the church, which it calls "especially, the holy temple" (Catechism of the Catholic Church 756).

No Orthodox council has ruled on the meaning of Ezekiel 40-48. The Greek fathers read the temple as the church, and the Orthodox liturgy reads Ezekiel 43:27-44:4 on feasts of the Mother of God, taking the closed gate as a picture of Mary (see the card at 44:2).

traditions.q: Who are Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38-39), and is the battle the same as in Revelation 20?
views: Ezekiel 38-39 describes a future attack on restored Israel by a northern power. The note on chapter 38 in the Scofield Reference Bible says the primary reference is to the northern (European) powers, headed by Russia. It reads Revelation 20:8 as a different, later rebellion at the end of the thousand years, whose peoples are called by the same names.

Historic (non-dispensational) premillennialists, such as George Eldon Ladd, hold that Christ returns before a thousand-year reign on earth, and that Revelation 20:7-10 is the last revolt of the nations at its end. Ladd reads John as taking the names Gog and Magog from Ezekiel to describe that final assault, not a Russian-led war earlier in the story.

Augustine (City of God 20.11) read Gog and Magog in Revelation 20 as the nations all over the earth, the church's last enemies, not as the names of two peoples. The amillennial view common among Reformed teachers (for example Anthony Hoekema, The Bible and the Future) follows him: Ezekiel's own battle is then a picture of the same hostility and the same defeat. Postmillennial teachers, who expect a long age of the gospel's success first, take the last revolt of Revelation 20 as the final defeat of the world's opposition, and they differ on whether Ezekiel 38-39 was already fulfilled or points to that revolt.

The Church has not defined who Gog is. On Revelation 20 the Catechism rejects teaching that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years before the final judgment (Catechism of the Catholic Church 676), and Catholic teaching has followed Augustine in reading the thousand years as the present age of the church and the revolt of Gog and Magog as the nations' last assault on it (City of God 20.11).

No Orthodox council has ruled on who Gog is. Andrew of Caesarea, whose Commentary on the Apocalypse became the standard Greek one, reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the time of the church and Gog and Magog as the nations that rise against it at the end, not as one people on a map.

Article 17 of the Augsburg Confession rejects the "Jewish opinions" that the godly will take over the kingdom of the world before the resurrection, which rules out a thousand-year earthly reign. On Ezekiel itself, Luther's 1530 preface to chapters 38-39 read Gog as the Turk, the great enemy of Christendom in his day. The confession does not say who Gog is.
